items.name: Smokey Bear
clues: A mascot who has been telling people off, very politely, for more than eighty years.
The US Forest Service, with help from the advertising industry’s wartime council, in 1944.
The first poster showed him in jeans and a ranger’s hat, pouring a bucket of water on a campfire.
In 1950 a real cub with burned paws was rescued after a fire in New Mexico. He lived for 26 years at the National Zoo in Washington.
In 2001 his famous line changed by one word so that it covered grassland too: “Only you can prevent wildfires.”
He’s a bear, his name sounds like what a fire makes, and he says: “Only you can prevent forest fires.”

items.name: Dumb Ways to Die
clues: Cute, catchy and full of deaths. It looks like a children’s cartoon until you listen to the words.
A railway company in Melbourne, Australia, in November 2012.
Little colourful blobs who come to silly ends, like keeping a rattlesnake as a pet or poking a stick at a grizzly bear.
The video keeps the dumbest ways for last: the ones that happen on station platforms and level crossings.
It won a record five Grand Prix at the Cannes Lions advertising festival in 2013, and became a mobile game.
Its song’s title: “Dumb … to …”. Fill in the two missing words.

items.name: I Want You
aliases: i want you for us army
i want you for u.s. army
clues: Possibly the most copied poster in history. Wherever you stand in the room, it seems to be talking to you.
The United States, 1917, the year the country entered the First World War.
A stern older man with a white goatee, pointing his finger straight at you.
The illustrator had no time to hire a model, so he drew his own face in a mirror and added some wrinkles.
About four million copies were printed in the First World War. It was inspired by a British poster from 1914 of Britain’s war minister pointing at you.
A man in a top hat covered in stars, the symbol of the USA, says three words to you.

items.name: We Can Do It!
clues: Today it’s on T-shirts, mugs and protest signs. When it was made, hardly anyone saw it.
Pittsburgh, 1943, in the middle of the Second World War.
A woman in a blue work shirt and a red polka-dot headscarf rolls up her sleeve and shows you her muscles.
An electrical company’s war production committee put it up in its own factories, for just two weeks.
It was forgotten for almost forty years, rediscovered in the early 1980s and turned into a feminist icon.
People call her “Rosie the Riveter”, although she only got that name later. Her speech bubble has three words.

items.name: Movember
clues: Every year, for one month, lots of men look slightly different, and that's the whole point.
It started with a small group of friends in Melbourne, Australia, in 2003.
Office photos, team selfies and charity pages full of men with new hair on their faces.
The money raised goes to men's health: prostate and testicular cancer, and mental health.
You grow a moustache for thirty days and ask friends to sponsor it.
Its name mixes “moustache” with the eleventh month of the year.

items.name: Ice Bucket Challenge
clues: For a few weeks one summer, it seemed as if every famous person in the world was getting very cold on camera.
Social media, in July and August 2014, starting in the United States.
Shaky phone videos of people standing in their gardens, bracing themselves and then screaming.
Once someone nominated you, you had 24 hours to film yourself, donate, or both, and then nominate three more people.
It raised money for research into ALS, the disease Stephen Hawking had. The ALS Association passed 100 million dollars within about a month.
Fill a bucket with water and ice, then pour it over your own head.
